title: Search inside a design critique tool
excerpt: Search should open the frame at the note someone remembers, on the version where it was written. Unresolved notes outrank old ones, and files they cannot see should not appear.
alt: A clothing shop interior with folded shirts, hanging jackets, shelves, and pendant lights, a room you scan for one garment.
caption: The racks are the index. The garment is the result. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should critique search return?
faqs.answer: A file with its thumbnail and version, or a comment's first line on that file, opening at the pin. Rank unresolved notes and current versions first unless the query names an older label. Recents help when the box is empty. View events are not results.

faqs.question: How do old versions show up in search?
faqs.answer: A query that names a version should open that version and say if a newer draft exists. If the pin's region was lost, open the version where the note was made and offer the jump forward. Dropping someone on a new frame with the note missing feels like data loss.

faqs.question: What should search refuse to index?
faqs.answer: Files and internal notes the person cannot open, plus view events and pixel guesses. Say that contract under the box. A miss should say nothing matched and offer recent files, not a pile of weak cousins that waste the meeting.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A small team opens design critique tool search ux when the file list, the version switcher, and the pins on the canvas have not found the note or the screen they need. Show matches in their words, and show a way back to the frame.

Nielsen Norman Group's study of how long people stay found that people often leave within 10 to 20 seconds, and that they read only about a quarter of the text even when they remain. A search hit that is a paragraph about collaboration will be skipped. The frame name, the comment's first line, and the version will not.

## What a small team types

They type a file name, a version label, a teammate, or a phrase from a comment. "Homepage." "After legal." "Sam." "The hero is doing too much." They are trying to return to a decision, usually because a meeting is starting or a build is about to include the wrong screen. They are not browsing a catalog of your features.

Sometimes they type the words they remember, which are not the words you stored. They search "nav" and the note says "header." They search "the blue one" and the file is called "Homepage Thursday." Close matches and recent files matter more here than a perfect index, because the corpus is small and the memory is visual.

Do not make search the way someone opens this week's review. A small team has a handful of active files. Those belong on the home, as frames, not as a command palette. Search is the repair when the home is a graveyard of Final-final, or when the note is one line inside a long review. If people must search to find the only file that matters, fix the home.

## Matches in their language

Lead with the thing they would recognize on the wall. A file result is the frame thumbnail, the name they gave it, and the version. A comment result is the sentence, the file, and the version it sits on. A person result is the unresolved notes that person wrote or was asked to answer. Put the matched words in that title. A highlight inside a timestamp will not be seen.

Rank unresolved notes above resolved ones, and current versions above old drafts, unless the query names an old label. "After legal" should return that version even if a newer draft exists, and the row should say whether a newer draft is now the default. Opening an old version without saying so is how a team edits the past by mistake.

Group by kind when the word matches more than one. Files, then open comments, then people. A flat list will put a file named Sam above the notes Sam still owes. Kind is the better sort. Within comments, put open above resolved, and say the status in the row so they do not open a finished note expecting work.

When the box is empty, show recent files and recent notes for this person. Four items. Recents teach the shape of a result and catch the reviewer who came back from a notification and lost the thread. They are not a feed of everyone else's activity. "Sam viewed" is not a search result. Do not put it here.

## A way back to the frame

Every comment hit should open on the frame, at that pin, with the note open, and a way back to the results with the query intact. The point of the search was the place. A comment detail page with no frame is a quote removed from the work, and the team will not trust it.

If the pin's region was lost in a later version, open the version where the note was made, and say that. "This note is on Thursday's draft. The current draft is Friday." Offer the jump to Friday. Do not drop them on Friday with the note missing and no explanation. That feels like data loss.

If they cannot open the file, the row should say why, or the row should not exist. "Client review. You are not on this link." A result that fails after the click feels broken, which is the feeling search is supposed to repair, not create. For a small team, omitting secret files is usually better than teasing them. The existence of an unreleased brand exploration may itself be the secret.

Keep the canvas they came from if they were mid-comment. Search that navigates away and discards a draft will be used once and then avoided. A panel over the file, or a promise that the draft is kept, is part of search quality. Speed is the other part. The set of files is small. The results should feel immediate. A theatrical loading state on top of fifty notes is a mismatch.

## Versions, filters, and false empties

Version and status are filters, and they should be visible chips. "Homepage · unresolved · this version." An empty list should name the chips. "No unresolved notes on Friday's draft. Include Thursday, or clear the status." One action to widen. A sticky filter from a previous file is a particularly sharp bug, because the team will think Friday's critique was deleted. Announce the filter or reset it when the file changes.

Empty, failed, and filtered are three sentences. "No notes match 'nav.'" "Search did not run." "You are looking at resolved notes only." Use the right one. A drawing of binoculars cannot.

Synonyms can be gentle. If they search "nav" and a note says "header," you may show it as a related word, labeled, not as a silent substitution that makes them doubt their memory. With a small corpus, showing a few related hits under the exact hits is more honest than a clever ranker that hides the reason.

A review in progress should be searchable by the decision word the team actually uses, even when that word never made it into the filename. If the notes say "shorten the hero" across three comments, that phrase is a better query than the file's export name. Index those lines. Boost the open ones. The team is looking for the argument, and the argument lives in the notes.

People search for the decision, not the pixel. Index the comment text, the file name, the version label, and the names of the people on the review. Do not index "viewed" events, cursor coordinates, or the contents of files they cannot open. Say the contract under the box. "Files you can open, and the notes on them." If internal notes exist, index them only for roles who can read them. A client search that returns an internal argument is a serious leak with a mild icon.

## Thumbnails earn the click

A critique search without a picture is only half a result. The team remembers the layout, not the filename. A small thumbnail of the frame, cropped to the pin when the hit is a comment, will outperform a clever snippet. Keep the thumbnail honest: the version the note belongs to, not the latest frame with an old sentence pasted on. If the thumbnail fails to load, the text result should still stand. The picture is the accelerator. The name and the sentence are the record.

Do not search inside the pixels. "Find the blue button" is a wish, and shipping a vague visual search that returns random frames will train the team to ignore the box. Search the words they typed and the titles they gave. If a frame has no title, prompt for one on upload so later search has something true to return. Untitled-1 is a wound you can prevent in the cabinet and feel in the search results a week later.

When several frames share a name, the thumbnail plus the version label is the disambiguation. "Homepage" three times, with three pictures, is a useful result. "Homepage" three times, with three timestamps, is a guessing game. Small teams can handle a short list. They should not have to open each one to see if the hero is the old one.

## Review five real lines

Use last week's file. Search a word from an unresolved note, a word from a resolved one, a version label, a teammate who owes a reply, and a word that should miss. The unresolved note should open on the pin. The version label should not quietly show a newer frame. The teammate search should list what they owe, not their biography. The miss should say nothing matched, and offer recent files, not a pile of weakly related comments that waste the meeting.

Settings are the other door, when the issue is not finding a note but how notifications, defaults, and required approvers behave. [Settings in a design critique tool](/blog/settings-in-a-design-critique-tool) is the next piece. Treat that area as a cabinet so search stays a way to find the work, not a way to configure the product.

If your team still screenshots the frame into a doc because old notes are impossible to find, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring one file and the phrase you wish you could type. The right hit is a frame with the note open, not a list of activity.
